hints: Identify all forces parallel to the plane: $T\cos 20^\circ$ pulling up, friction $F = 5\text{ N}$ down, and weight component $mg\sin 30^\circ$ down.
Apply Newton's second law along the plane: $T\cos 20^\circ - F - mg\sin 30^\circ = ma$.
Substitute $m = 2\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $F = 5\text{ N}$, and $a = 1.2\text{ m s}^{-2}$, then divide by $\cos 20^\circ$ to find $T$.
walkthrough:
State Newton's second law of motion along the direction of motion (up the inclined plane):
$$F_{\text{net}} = ma$$

Identify each force acting parallel to the incline:
- Component of tension acting up the plane: $T\cos 20^\circ$
- Opposing friction force acting down the plane: $F = 5\text{ N}$
- Component of gravity acting down the slope: $mg\sin 30^\circ$

Write the resulting equation of motion:
$$T\cos 20^\circ - F - mg\sin 30^\circ = ma$$

Substitute the given numerical values: $m = 2\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $F = 5\text{ N}$, and $a = 1.2\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$T\cos 20^\circ - 5 - (2)(10)\sin 30^\circ = (2)(1.2)$$

Add 15 to both sides, then divide by $\cos 20^\circ$ to solve for $T$:
$$T\cos 20^\circ = 17.4$$
$$T = \frac{17.4}{\cos 20^\circ} \approx \frac{17.4}{0.939693} \approx 18.5167\text{ N}$$
$$T = 18.5\text{ N}\quad (\text{to 3 significant figures})$$

hints: Resolve forces perpendicular to the inclined plane in equilibrium to find the normal reaction $R$.
Set up $R + T\sin 20^\circ = mg\cos 30^\circ$ and substitute your value of $T$ to evaluate $R$.
Apply the limiting friction formula $F = \mu R$ with $F = 5\text{ N}$ to calculate the coefficient $\mu$.
walkthrough:
State the equilibrium condition perpendicular to the inclined plane (there is no acceleration perpendicular to the slope):
$$\sum F_{\perp} = 0$$

Identify the three forces perpendicular to the plane:
- Normal reaction $R$ pointing outwards from the surface
- Component of rope tension away from the surface: $T\sin 20^\circ$
- Component of gravity pushing into the surface: $mg\cos 30^\circ$

Form the equilibrium equation and solve for $R$:
$$R + T\sin 20^\circ = mg\cos 30^\circ$$
$$R = mg\cos 30^\circ - T\sin 20^\circ$$

State the formula for limiting friction on a sliding object:
$$F = \mu R$$

Rearrange to solve for $\mu$, then substitute $F = 5\text{ N}$ and $R = 10.9874\text{ N}$:
$$\mu = \frac{F}{R} = \frac{5}{10.9874} \approx 0.45507$$
$$\mu = 0.455\quad (\text{to 3 significant figures})$$

hints: Calculate the normal reaction $R$ perpendicular to the plane with $T = 15\text{ N}$, then find the maximum available friction $F_{\text{max}} = \mu R$ using $\mu = 0.8$.
Calculate the net force tending to move the block up the plane before friction acts: $T\cos 20^\circ - mg\sin 30^\circ$.
Compare the net upward pulling force with the maximum available friction to determine whether the block will move up the plane.
walkthrough: State the approach: to test whether the block moves up the plane, we calculate the net upward force pulling the block and compare it with the maximum limiting friction the rough surface can provide.

First, resolve forces perpendicular to the inclined plane to determine the normal reaction force $R$:
$$R + T\sin 20^\circ = mg\cos 30^\circ$$
$$R = mg\cos 30^\circ - T\sin 20^\circ$$

Calculate the maximum limiting friction force $F_{\text{max}}$ using the given coefficient $\mu = 0.8$:
$$F_{\text{max}} = \mu R = 0.8 \times 12.1902 = 9.7522\text{ N}$$

Next, calculate the net force acting up the plane before friction acts (tension component up the plane minus weight component down the plane):
$$F_{\text{up}} = T\cos 20^\circ - mg\sin 30^\circ$$
$$T\cos 20^\circ = 15 \times 0.939693 = 14.0954\text{ N}$$
$$mg\sin 30^\circ = (2)(10)(0.5) = 10\text{ N}$$
$$F_{\text{up}} = 14.0954 - 10 = 4.0954\text{ N}$$

Compare the two values:
$$4.0954\text{ N} < 9.7522\text{ N}$$
$$\text{Because the net upward force }(4.10\text{ N})\text{ is less than the maximum limiting friction }(9.75\text{ N}),\text{ friction prevents any motion, so } B \text{ will not move up the plane.}$$
